names.name: flat
names.said: 'Flats or drums?' — and most places cannot answer it.

etymology.root: the adjective flat, turned into a noun for the piece it describes; the competing name wingette is wing + -ette, the same diminutive that built drumette
etymology.note: Two words, one piece. The National Chicken Council calls it "the mid-section or 'flat'"; Wikipedia's poultry article gives it as "the 'wingette' (also called the 'flat')". USDA's grading captions use neither, labelling it 'Grade A Second Segment Wing Portion (Wing Flat)'. *Inference —* wingette reads as packer's English and flat as counter English, and the counter is winning.

text.what: Middle segment, two bones with a gap between them, and more skin per bite than any other piece of a chicken. Flat because it is — it lies down in the fryer basket and comes out on one plane. Two per bird.
text.how: Twist out the smaller bone, then pull the larger one, and the meat comes free in a strip; people who order all flats are usually doing that. More surface means more crust and more sauce clinging, which is the case its partisans make against the drumette.

kin.as: The other half of the split, and the side of the argument this one is against.
One of the two pieces a menu means when it says wing.
The order that asks for nothing but these.
Attached to this piece until somebody cuts it off; a few kitchens leave it on.
The argument this word is the other half of.
Where the second cut goes, and why this piece keeps two bones.
Bagged with the drumettes and sold as one product.
